title: Use appropriate communication skills, conventions and structures for specific purposes and situations

lessons.title: Speaking and listening at work
lessons.html:
Choose the right way to communicate

We do not speak to everyone in the same way. You talk differently to a friend at home, to your supervisor, to a customer and at a community meeting. Good communicators think about three things:

  • Purpose: why am I speaking? To ask, explain, complain, report or greet?
  • Audience: who am I speaking to? A child, a manager, a visitor?
  • Situation: where am I? In the field, in a meeting, on the phone?

Speaking clearly

  1. Greet the person politely and use their name or title.
  2. Say the main point first.
  3. Use short sentences and simple words.
  4. Give facts: what, where, when, who.
  5. Check that the person understood. Ask: Is that clear?

Example: Good morning, Mr Dlamini. The pump at dam two is leaking. I saw it at seven o'clock. Water is running onto the road. Can you send someone to fix it?

Listening well

  • Look at the person and stop what you are doing.
  • Do not interrupt. Let them finish.
  • Ask questions if you do not understand.
  • Repeat the main points back: So you want me to move the sheep to camp five after lunch?

Body language

We also communicate without words: our face, eyes, hands and voice. Standing with folded arms and looking away can show you are not interested. A calm voice and open posture show respect. Remember that body language can mean different things in different cultures; for example, in some cultures young people avoid direct eye contact with elders out of respect.

On the phone or two-way radio

Say who you are and where you are, speak slowly, keep it short, and confirm the message at the end.

lessons.title: Writing for different purposes
lessons.html:
Conventions and structures

Conventions are the accepted rules for a type of communication. Structure is the order in which the information is set out. Each kind of writing has its own conventions.

A short message or note

Include the date, who it is for, the message, and your name. Example:

12 March. To: Sipho. The bakkie needs diesel before Thursday. From: Thandi.

A simple report

A report tells someone what happened. Use this structure:

  1. Date, time and place.
  2. What happened, in the order it happened.
  3. Who was involved.
  4. What was done about it.
  5. Your name and signature.

Write only facts, not guesses. For an injury or accident, report straight away to your supervisor and write down the details as soon as possible.

Filling in forms

  • Read the whole form first.
  • Use a pen and write in clear block letters if asked.
  • Fill in every part. Write N/A if something does not apply.
  • Check your ID number, dates and phone numbers.
  • Sign and date where needed.

A formal letter

PartWhat to write
Your address and dateTop right
Receiver's name and addressLeft, below
GreetingDear Mr Nkosi / Dear Sir or Madam
Subject lineRe: Application for leave
BodyShort paragraphs: why you write, details, what you ask for
ClosingYours faithfully or Yours sincerely, then your name and signature

Messages on a phone

WhatsApp and SMS at work should still be polite and clear. Do not use rude words or send messages to the wrong group. Do not share private farm information.

Meetings

At a meeting, wait your turn to speak, keep to the topic, and respect the chairperson. Someone writes the minutes so everyone remembers what was decided.

Key points

  • Think about purpose, audience and situation before you communicate.
  • Speak clearly, give facts and check understanding.
  • Listen without interrupting and repeat the main points back.
  • Each type of writing has its own conventions and structure.
  • Reports must contain facts, dates, times and your name.
